﴿Ha Mim﴾. The discussion of the disjoined letters (huruf al-hija', the letters that open some surahs) has already been covered. The word "Ha Mim" has the specific meaning: "humma al-amr," that is, the matter was decreed, meaning it was determined. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Alif Lam Ra", "Ha Mim", and "Nun" are the letters of "al-Rahman."

{Tanzil al-Kitab} (ﷺ) — the revelation of the Book. Mentioned in Surah al-Zumar.

Note: The passage given is brief, so the translation follows it directly.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 3:

﴿Dhi al-Tawl﴾ means: the Possessor of bounty and favour. It has also been said: al-Tawl means wealth and abundance.

﴿So let not their movement about in the land deceive you.﴾ He made "لا يغررك" (let not deceive you) mean "لا يحزنك" (let not grieve you). So it is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelievers.
﴿The factions﴾ are meant to include ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others. ﴿To seize him﴾, i.e., to kill him. ﴿To refute﴾, i.e., to nullify the truth by means of it.
﴿Ḥaqqat kalimatu rabbika﴾ means: the decree of your Lord has become binding (wajaba qaḍāʾuhu).

﴿And those around it﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf, coordination) with ﴿those who carry the Throne﴾, and ﴿and believe in Him﴾. If it is asked: what is the benefit of His words ﴿and believe in Him﴾, when it is known that the bearers of the Throne and those around it believe in God? The answer is that this shows the excellence and nobility of faith. Al-Zamakhshari said this, and said: there is another benefit in it, namely that the bearers of the Throne know God through reflection and inference (naẓar wa-istidlāl), like the rest of creation, not through seeing. This is his inclination toward the doctrine of the Muʿtazila (the rationalist school) regarding the impossibility of seeing God.

﴿You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge﴾. The original sentence was: "Your mercy and Your knowledge encompassed everything." The encompassing, in meaning, is ascribed to mercy and knowledge, and they were ascribed to God Most High in wording only to emphasise the description of God with them, as if His essence were mercy and knowledge that encompass everything.

{And protect them from evil deeds} It is possible that the meaning is: protect them from the evil deeds themselves, so that they do not commit them; or the meaning is: protect them from the requital of evil deeds, so that You do not hold them accountable for them.

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out to: the hatred of Allah is greater than your hatred of yourselves﴾. Al-maqt (hatred) is the loathing that is caused by a sin or a defect. This state befalls the disbelievers when they enter the Fire, for when they enter it they loathe themselves, meaning some of them loathe others. It is also possible that each of them loathes himself, and then the angels call out to them and say: Allah's loathing of you in the world for your disbelief is greater than your loathing of yourselves today.

So His words, ﴿لمقت الله﴾ (the hatred of Allah), are a maṣdar (verbal noun) in an annexed construction (muḍāf) to its agent, and its object has been omitted, because the object of "your hatred" (maqtikum) indicates it. His words ﴿إِذْ تُدْعَوْنَ﴾ (when you were being called) are a ẓarf (adverb of time), and its ʿāmil (governing element) is ﴿مَقْتُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ (the hatred of Allah), in terms of meaning, not according to the rules of grammar, because the verbal noun "maqt Allāh" cannot govern it in grammatical terms, since it is not permissible to separate it from part of its complement. Therefore one must posit a governing element for the adverb. On this basis some scholars permitted pausing (waqf) at His words ﴿أَنفُسَكُـمْ﴾ (yourselves) and beginning (ibtidāʾ) with the adverb, but this is weak, because what is observed is the meaning. Al-Zamakhsharī made ﴿مَقْتُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ the governing element of the adverb and did not take the separation into account.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 11–12:

﴿They said: "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice."﴾ This verse is like His saying: ﴿And you were dead and He brought you to life; then He causes you to die, then brings you to life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. The first death is the state of their being non-existent, or their being in the loins (asla') or in the wombs (arham). The second death is the well-known death, and the first life is the life of this world, and the second life is the life of resurrection on the Day of Judgment. It has also been said: the first life is the life of this world, and the second is life in the grave, and the first death is the well-known death, and the second death is after the life of the grave. But this is a corrupt view, because life is necessary for resurrection, so life would come three times.

If it is asked: how does their saying "You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice" connect with what precedes it? The answer: they used to deny resurrection in the world, so when they entered the Fire they loathed themselves for that, and then they acknowledged it so that they might please God by their acknowledgment. Thus their saying "You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice" is an acknowledgment of resurrection in the most complete manner, hoping that they might be delivered from the loathing (maqt) with which God loathed them, since they used to be called to Islam and would disbelieve. ﴿So we confess our sins﴾: the fa' here is a connecting particle (rabitah) whose meaning is causation (tasabbub). If it is asked: how can their saying "You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice" be a cause of their confession of sins? The answer: they used to disbelieve in resurrection, so when they saw that death and life had been repeated upon them, they knew that God is able to resurrect, so they confessed their sins, which were the denial of resurrection and the sins that their denial had made necessary for them, for whoever does not believe in the Hereafter does not care about falling into sins. ﴿That is because when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved﴾: the ba' here is causal (sababiyyah) for the purpose of explaining the reason. The demonstrative "dhalikum" may refer to the punishment they are in, or to God's loathing of them, or their loathing of themselves. The best view is that it refers to what the context of the speech requires, since when they said ﴿Is there any way out?﴾, it was as if it were said to them: there is no way out, so the demonstrative in His saying ﴿dhalikum﴾ refers to their not leaving the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 13:

﴿He shows you His signs﴾: that is, the indications of Him in His creation and the miracles of His messengers. ﴿And sends down for you provision from the sky﴾: that is, the rain.

Rafi' al-darajat (Exalted in degrees). It is possible that the meaning is "high in degrees," so it would mean "the Exalted," or "raising the degrees of His servants in Paradise and in this world." Yulqi al-ruh (He casts the Spirit) means the revelation. Min amrihi (by His command) may refer to amr in the sense of one of the matters (umur), or amr in the sense of a command. In the first case, min is either partitive (lil-tab'id) or indicates the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah); in the second case, it is either indicating the starting point or means bi (with). Yawm al-talaq (the Day of Meeting) means the Day of Resurrection, and it was so named because the creatures meet on it. It was also said: because the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth meet on it. It was also said: because the created beings meet their Lord on it. The subject of yunzir (to warn) is a pronoun referring either to "whomever He wills," or to the Spirit, or to God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 16:

﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ This is from the speech of God, Exalted, as a question put to creation on the Day of Resurrection (taqrir). They answer Him and say: ﴿To God, the One, the Subduer.﴾ It has also been said: rather, it is He who answers Himself, because the creatures remain silent out of awe of Him. And it has been said: the one who says ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ is an angel.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 18:

﴿The Day of the Imminent (Yawm al-Azifah)﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, and its meaning is "the near one." ﴿When the hearts rise up to the throats﴾ means that the hearts have ascended from the chests out of intense fear until they reach the throats. It is possible that this is literal, or it is a metaphor by which intense fear is expressed. Al-hanajir is the plural of hanjarah, which is the throat. ﴿Choking with grief (kazimin)﴾ means grieving intensely, like His saying: ﴿and he was filled with grief (fa-huwa kazim)﴾ [Yusuf: 84]. It was also said that the meaning is: they suppress their grief, hoping to conceal it, while the condition overwhelms them. Its placement as a circumstantial accusative (hal) is from the people of the hearts, because its meaning is "the hearts of people," or from the object in "warn them," or from the hearts. Its plural is formed as a masculine plural because it was described with suppression (kazm), which is one of the actions of rational beings. ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend (hamim)﴾ meaning a compassionate friend, ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed.﴾ This may mean the negation of intercession and of obeying an intercessor, or the negation of a particular kind of obedience. It is like your saying: "No righteous man came to me," where you negate righteousness, even though a non-righteous man may have come to you. The first interpretation is better, because the disbelievers have no one who will intercede for them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 19:

﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ meaning the furtive glance. Al-khā'inah (the treachery) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of al-khiyānah (treachery), or it is an attribute of the glance. This statement is connected to what preceded concerning the mention of God, and within it he interjected a description of the Resurrection, since he digressed to it from His saying: ﴿that He may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [Ghafir: 15].
[Qur'an 40:23] "And a clear authority" — an evident proof, namely the miracles.
They said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him." This killing is different from the killing they had carried out earlier, before Moses was born.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 26:

﴿And Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord."﴾ The meaning: he does not care about Moses' supplication to his Lord, and he does not fear any consequence if he kills him. It appears from his words ﴿Leave me﴾ that among the people there were those who opposed him regarding the killing of Moses, and this indicates that Pharaoh's affair had become unsettled through the manifestation of Moses' miracles. ﴿Or that he may bring about corruption in the land﴾ meaning the corruption of their circumstances in this world. Or "that he may bring about," and it is read with the waw alone, and "yuzhira" with a fathah on the ya', and "al-fasad" in the nominative as the subject, and with a ḍammah on the ya' and "al-fasad" in the accusative as the object.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 27:

﴿And Moses said: "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ The verse: When Moses heard what Pharaoh had resolved to do, namely to kill him, he sought refuge in God, and God protected him from him. And he said: ﴿from every arrogant one﴾, so that it includes Pharaoh and others, and so that there is in it a description of someone other than Pharaoh with that ugly attribute.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 28–29:**

﴿And a believing man from among the family of Pharaoh said﴾. It is said: the name of this man was Habib, and it is said: Hizqil (Ezekiel), and it is said: Shamun, with the letter shin pointed (with a dot above). It is narrated that this believing man was a cousin of Pharaoh. Thus, His saying "from among the family of Pharaoh" is a *sifa* (qualifier, descriptive attribute) of "the believing man." It is said that he was from the Children of Israel. Then, according to this view, His saying ﴿from among the family of Pharaoh﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿who concealed his faith﴾. The first view is more likely (*arjah*), because it does not require any *taqdim wa ta'khir* (fronting and postponing of words). It is also supported by His saying ﴿so who will help us against the might of Allah?﴾, because this is the speech of a close and compassionate person. And because the Children of Israel at that time were humiliated, such that none of them could speak with words like these.

The phrase ﴿an yaqula﴾ (that he says) is in the position of the *maf'ul li-ajlihi* (object of purpose, adverbial of reason). Its estimated meaning is: "Will you kill him because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?"

﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie﴾: that is, if Musa is lying in his claim to prophethood, his lie will not harm you, so why do you kill him? If it is asked: how could he say "and if he is a liar" after he had already believed in him? The answer is that he did not say it in the manner of denying him; rather, he said it in the manner of supposition and assumption, and by that he intended to argue with his people. So he divided the matter of Musa into two parts, in order to establish the proof against them for abandoning his killing, in each of the two cases.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you﴾. It is said: "some" here means "all," but that is far-fetched. He said "some" and did not say "all," even though what would befall them is all of what he promises them, in order to soften his speech with them, to keep away from partisanship for Musa, and to show sincere advice to Pharaoh and his people, so that there is hope they will accept the truth.

{"Translation"}

"﴿And the one who believed said﴾: He is the believing man mentioned earlier. It was also said that he is Musa, peace be upon him, but this is far-fetched. They only imagined that because he openly declared faith here, whereas the speech of the believer earlier was not explicit; rather, it contained allusion (tawriyah) and gentleness toward his people, since he was concealing his faith. The answer: he concealed his faith at the beginning, then declared it openly afterward, and confronted them with clear boldness, once he had put his trust in God, as God recounted of his speech up to His words ﴿So you will remember what I say to you, and I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44]."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 32–33:

﴿The Day of Calling Out (yawm al-tanad)﴾: al-Tanad means the Day of Resurrection, and it was so named because the caller calls out to the people, as in His words: ﴿The Day We shall call every people﴾ [al-Isra: 71]. It was also said that it is because some of them call out to others: the people of Paradise call out ﴿that we have indeed found what our Lord promised us to be true﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and the people of the Fire call out: ﴿Pour upon us some water﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. ﴿The Day you turn back fleeing﴾, meaning departing toward the Fire. It was also said: fleeing from the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 32–33:

﴿The Day of Calling Out (yawm al-tanad)﴾: al-Tanad means the Day of Resurrection, and it was so named because the caller calls out to the people, as in His words: ﴿The Day We shall call every people﴾ [al-Isra: 71]. It was also said that it is because some of them call out to others: the people of Paradise call out ﴿that we have indeed found what our Lord promised us to be true﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and the people of the Fire call out: ﴿Pour upon us some water﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. ﴿The Day you turn back fleeing﴾, meaning departing toward the Fire. It was also said: fleeing from the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 34:

﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾. It is said: he is Joseph son of Jacob (Ya'qub). It is also said: he is Joseph son of Abraham (Ibrahim) son of Joseph son of Jacob. The clear proofs that Joseph brought are not specified for us. It is disputed whether the Pharaoh of Moses reached him, or whether it was another Pharaoh before him, since every ruler of Egypt was called Pharaoh. ﴿And you said: Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾. Their statement does not indicate that they believed in the prophethood of Joseph; rather, what they meant was: no one has come claiming prophethood after Joseph. This is what Ibn 'Atiyyah said. al-Zamakhshari said: it is only a denial of a messenger after him, joined with a denial of his own prophethood.

**﴿Those who dispute﴾** is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for "*musrif murtab*" (extravagant and doubting). It is permissible for a plural to substitute for a singular because the singular here has the meaning of a plural, as if he had said: "every extravagant person." **﴿Greatly hateful it is﴾**: the subject (*fa'il*) of *kabura* (is great) is the verbal noun (*masdar*) of *yujadiluna* (they dispute), which is *jidal*. Al-Zamakhshari said: the subject is a pronoun referring to "the one who is extravagant" (*man huwa musrif*).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 40, verses 36–37:

﴿al-asbab (the means)﴾ Here it means the ways (طرق, turuq), and it was said: the doors (أبواب, abwab). He repeated it for emphasis (تفخيم, tafkhim) and for clarification (بيان, bayan).

﴿and I may look up (fa-atṭali῾a)﴾ It is read in the nominative (بالرفع, bil-raf῾) as a conjunction (عطف, ʿatf) on "أبلغ" (ablugh), and in the accusative (بالنصب, bil-nasb) by the implied "أن" (an) after "لعل" (la῾alla), as the answer to it, because the expectation (الترجّي, al-tarajjي) is not binding. It is therefore like the wish (التمني, al-tamanni) in the accusative of its answer. We do not say that "لعل" has taken on the meaning of "ليت" (layta), as some grammarians (النجاة, al-nuhat) have said.

﴿destruction (تباب, tabab)﴾ That is, loss (خسران, khusran).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 39:

﴿Enjoyment﴾ meaning: one enjoys it for a little while. If it is asked: why did the believer repeat the call to his people several times? The answer: this is for the purpose of alerting them, and showing gentleness and sincere advice. If it is asked: why was the conjunction "wa" (and) used in his saying ﴿O my people﴾ in the third instance but not in the second? The answer: the second is an explanation and elaboration of the first, so it was not correct to join it to it by conjunction, unlike the third, which is a separate statement, so it was correct to join it to what precedes.

﴿That of which I have no knowledge﴾ means: I have no knowledge of His lordship (rububiyyah). The negation of knowledge here is the negation of what is known. It is as if he said: "and associate with Him that which is not a god." And if it is not a god, then knowledge of His lordship cannot be valid.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 43:

﴿Lā jarama﴾ means: there is no doubt and no question (lā budda wa-lā shakk). ﴿Laysa lahu da‘wah﴾ (he has no call). Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: He has no worth and no right; he is not owed to be called upon, as if he said: "Do you call me to worship something that has no standing in this world or in the Hereafter?" The wording may also bear the meaning: he has no established call, that is, no one is to be called to his worship.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 45:

﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾. This is evidence that whoever entrusts his affair to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has Allah with him.

﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it﴾. "The Fire" is in apposition (badal) to "the evil of the punishment," or it is the subject (mubtada') or the predicate (khabar) of an implied subject. Their being exposed to it is from the time of their death until the Day of Resurrection. That period is the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection), as shown by His saying, on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾. The People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) used this verse as evidence for the authenticity of what has been transmitted about the punishment of the grave. It is narrated that their spirits are in the bellies of black birds, which carry them to the Fire in the morning and in the evening, ﴿morning and evening﴾. It has been said that the meaning is: in every morning and evening of the days of this world. It has also been said that the meaning, by way of estimation, is: the period between morning and evening, because there is no morning or evening in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 49–50:

﴿To the guardians of Hell﴾ If it is said: why did He not say "those in the Fire to its guardians," so that He would have mentioned it without naming it? The answer is that mentioning Jahannam (Hell) carries a dread that is absent from mentioning a pronoun. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ This may be part of the speech of the guardians of Hell, in which case it is connected to His saying ﴿So call upon them﴾; or it may be part of the speech of Allah, Exalted, as a new sentence (isti'naf).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 49–50:

﴿To the guardians of Hell﴾ If it is said: why did He not say "those in the Fire to its guardians," so that He would have mentioned it without naming it? The answer is that mentioning Jahannam (Hell) carries a dread that is absent from mentioning a pronoun. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ This may be part of the speech of the guardians of Hell, in which case it is connected to His saying ﴿So call upon them﴾; or it may be part of the speech of Allah, Exalted, as a new sentence (isti'naf).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, We surely support Our messengers﴾. It is said: this is specific to those whom God has made victorious over the disbelievers, and it is not general, because among the prophets some were killed by their people, such as Zakariyya (Zechariah) and Yahya (John). The correct view is that it is general. The answer to what they have cited is that Zakariyya and Yahya were not among the messengers; they were among the prophets who were not sent as messengers. God only guaranteed the support of the messengers specifically, not the support of all the prophets. ﴿And the day when the witnesses stand up﴾: meaning the Day of Resurrection. Al-ashhad (the witnesses) is the plural of shahid or shahid, and it may carry the sense of presence (al-huduh), or the testimony over people, or testimony in the way of God. The more apparent meaning is testimony over people, based on His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [al-Nisa larr: 41].

The Qur'anic verse (﴿on the Day when no excuse of the wrongdoers will benefit them﴾) may be understood in two ways: either they will not offer excuses at all, or they will offer excuses but their excuses will not benefit them. The first interpretation is more preponderant (arjah), because of His saying: ﴿And it will not be permitted for them to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36], where He negates both the offering of excuses and their benefit from them.

﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning His promise to our master Muhammad (ﷺ) of victory and dominance over his disbelieving enemies. ﴿in the evening and the morning﴾. It was said: "al-'Ashi" is the prayer of 'Asr, and "al-Ibkar" is the prayer of Subh. It was also said: "al-'Ashi" is the period after 'Asr until sunset, and "al-Ibkar" is from the break of dawn until sunrise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, those who dispute about the signs of Allah﴾ means the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but pride﴾ i.e., arrogance and self-magnification, which prevents them from following you and from submitting to you. It has also been said: their pride is that they wanted prophethood for themselves and saw that they were more deserving of it. The first view is more apparent, because their desire for prophethood for themselves is envy, and the first is pride. ﴿They will never attain it﴾ i.e., they will not reach what their pride requires of prevailing over you and attaining prophethood. ﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾ i.e., seek refuge from their evil, for they are your enemies, and seek refuge from the likes of their state of pride and envy; and seek refuge in Allah in all your affairs without restriction.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 57–59:

﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ Here "al-khalq" (creation) is a verbal noun (masdar) in the genitive construction, with the verb's object as the first term (idafah to the object), and the intended meaning is to furnish proof for the resurrection (al-ba'th). This is because the Deity (al-Ilah) who created the heavens and the earth in their greatness is able to restore bodies after their annihilation. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a rebuke of the arrogant disbelievers, as if He had said: the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, so why do these people act arrogantly towards their Creator, when they are among the smallest and most insignificant of His creatures? The first view is more preferred (arjah), because of its occurrence in several places in the Qur'an, since He said after it: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it﴾. So He presented the proof first, then mentioned what the proof establishes.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 60:

﴿وَقَالَ رَبُّكُـمُ ٱدْعُونِيۤ أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ﴾ ["And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you."] Here, "du'a" (supplication, invocation) means asking and turning eagerly to Allah, and this is a promise made conditional upon His will (mashi'a), which is the agreement of divine decree (qadar) with whoever He wills to respond to. It has also been said that "ud'uni" here means "u'buduni" (worship Me), based on His saying after it: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبَادَتِي﴾ ["Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me..."], and on the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Du'a is worship," and then he recited the verse. According to this view, ﴿أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ﴾ ["I will respond to you"] means "I will forgive you or give you your rewards." The first view is more apparent, and His saying ﴿يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبَادَتِي﴾ ["too proud to worship Me"] would mean "too proud to turn to Me in asking," as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, Allah becomes angry with him." As for the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "Du'a is worship," its meaning is that supplication and turning to Allah is itself worship, because in du'a the servant's dependence (iftiqar) and humble submission (tadarru') before Allah become manifest. ﴿دَاخِرِينَ﴾ ["humbled"] means abased, lowly.
﴿So that you may rest therein﴾ — mentioned in [Surah Yunus, 10:67].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 64–65:

﴿And provided you with good things﴾. He means delicious things (al-mustalidhdhat), because when the mention of "good things" (al-tayyibat) comes in the context of bestowing favour, it means delicious things, and when it comes in the context of making lawful and unlawful, it means what is lawful (halal) and what is unlawful (haram). ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. This is connected to what precedes it. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari said so, and its implied sense is: "Call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him, saying: Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds." For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "Whoever says there is no god but God, let him say: Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds." It is also possible that "Praise be to God" is a new, independent statement (isti'naf).

Then He brings you out as a child. He intends the category (al-jins), which is why the word is singular, even though the address is to a group. Then that you may reach your **ashudd** (the age of full maturity; the word is mentioned in Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him: Yusuf [22]). The *lam* in *li-tablughū* is connected to a deleted verb whose sense is: then He lets you remain so that you may reach (maturity), and likewise so that you may become (...). Or, as for *li-tablughū ajalan musamman*, it is connected to another deleted element, whose sense is: He did that to you so that you may reach a specified term, which is death, or the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verses 69–72:

﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the verses of Allah?﴾ It means the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is also said that they are the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'), such as the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination) and others. This is rejected by His saying: ﴿who have denied the Book﴾, unless you take it as disconnected from what precedes it, which is far-fetched. ﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾: the governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" (when) is "yu'malun" (they will be made to know), and the past-tense time-frame has been placed in the position of the future to affirm the certainty of the matter. ﴿When the shackles [and chains are around their necks]﴾, meaning they will be dragged. And al-hamim is water of extreme heat. ﴿They will be dragged through boiling water﴾, meaning they will be dragged into al-hamim, the water of extreme heat. ﴿Then in the Fire they will be burned﴾. This is from your saying: "sajjartu al-tannur" (I heated the oven) when you filled it with fire; so the meaning is that they will enter it as firewood enters the oven. For this reason Mujahid said in his tafsir: "The fire will be kindled with them." ﴿Exulting﴾: from al-maraḥ, which is insolence and wantonness. It is also said: boasting and arrogance.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 40, verses 76–77:

﴿So evil is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ If it is said: the expected arrangement of the wording would be "evil is the entrance of the disbelievers," since "enter" (ادخلوا, udkhulū) was mentioned just before it. The answer: entering that is temporary, when it is with abiding (الخلود, al-khulud), has the meaning of dwelling (الثوى, al-thawa). ﴿So whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾. The original form of إما (imma) is إن نريك (in nurīka), and the extra particle ما (ma) was inserted after the conditional إن (in). The response to the condition is omitted, its estimated form being: if We show you some of the punishment We promise them, your eye will be comforted by that; and if We take you (in death) before that, then to Us they will return, and We will exact from them the most severe retribution.

﴿Among them are those We have related to you.﴾ It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah sent eight thousand messengers, and in another narration four thousand. In the hadith of Abu Dharr, the prophets are one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and among them the messengers are three hundred and thirteen. ﴿So when the command of Allah comes, it will be decided with truth.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: the command of Allah is the Resurrection. Its origin is a adverb of place, which was then used in the place of an adverb of time.

"Al-anʿam" (livestock) are camels, cattle, sheep and goats. His words ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾ refer to camels. ﴿And some of them you eat﴾ refers to their meat, and the benefits from them include milk, wool and other things. ﴿And that you may reach by them a need⁠⁠—⁠⁠﴾ refers to covering a great distance and carrying loads on camels. ﴿And you are carried﴾ means riding on them. He repeated it after His words ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾ because the first riding is the familiar one in villages and cities, and being carried on them refers to long journeys. This was stated by Ibn ʿAtiyyah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 40, verse 83:

﴿So they rejoiced in the knowledge they had﴾. The pronoun refers to the rejecting nations. There are several interpretations of their knowledge. The first is what they held to be true, namely that they would not be resurrected and would not be called to account. The second is their knowledge of the benefits of worldly life and the ways of earning them. The third is the knowledge of the philosophers who look down upon the sciences of the revealed laws. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the messengers, meaning they rejoiced in the knowledge God gave them and His laws, or in the knowledge they had that God would grant them victory over those who denied them. As for the pronoun in ﴿and what they used to mock overwhelmed them﴾, it refers to the disbelievers by consensus, and therefore it is preferred that the pronoun in ﴿they rejoiced﴾ also refers to them, so that the discourse is coherent. (Sunnat Allah) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq), and God knows best.
